title: Song of Solomon 7:10–13
context: The Beloved answers that she belongs to her beloved and that his desire is toward her, and invites him to go out to the fields and villages, to see the vineyards in bloom, and to receive the love and the precious fruits she has stored up for him. Both traditions read this as shared ground on mutual belonging and faithful love, and readers in both traditions also read the Song as a picture of God and his people or Christ and the church. Versification: English 6:13 is Hebrew 7:1, and English 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Speaker names (Lover, Beloved, Friends, Brothers) follow the WEB headings, which are interpretive and are not part of the Hebrew text.

verses.text: I am my beloved’s. His desire is toward me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Beloved says, “I am my beloved’s. His desire is toward me.” Arminian readers note the mutual belonging expressed here and in 2:16 and 6:3.

Some readers connect this with Genesis 3:16, where the same Hebrew word for desire appears, and see love restored to mutual delight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a confident sense of belonging. Allegorical readers in both traditions hear the believer’s assurance of being loved by God.

Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as a statement of faithful, mutual love.

verses.text: Come, my beloved! Let’s go out into the field. Let’s lodge in the villages.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Come, my beloved! Let’s go out into the field. Let’s lodge in the villages.” Arminian readers note that the Beloved takes the initiative in inviting him.

The Song gives both voices freedom to express love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the Beloved’s invitation as part of the mutuality of the Song.

Shared ground: both traditions note that love in the Song is expressed by both partners, and allegorical readers see an invitation to communion.

verses.text: Let’s go early up to the vineyards. Let’s see whether the vine has budded, its blossom is open, and the pomegranates are in flower. There I will give you my love.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Let’s see whether the vine has budded, its blossom is open, and the pomegranates are in flower. There I will give you my love.” Arminian readers note the springtime imagery (cf. 2:11–13).

The season of blossoming matches the joy of love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see creation’s renewal framing the couple’s love.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with restraint as faithful love offered freely, and they hear in the imagery the goodness of God’s creation.

verses.text: The mandrakes produce fragrance. At our doors are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which I have stored up for you, my beloved.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The mandrakes produce fragrance. At our doors are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which I have stored up for you.” Arminian readers note that mandrakes appear in Genesis 30:14–16 in the story of Rachel and Leah.

The image suggests something treasured and set aside.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the Beloved’s devotion in what she has “stored up” for him.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as faithful love reserved for one person, and allegorical readers see devotion offered to God.
